passages.t: Sweet lips, and a bitter end
passages.happening:
‘My son, pay attention to my wisdom; incline your ear to my insight’ (verse 1). The father warns his son about the forbidden woman. ‘Though the lips of the forbidden woman drip honey and her speech is smoother than oil, in the end she is bitter as wormwood, sharp as a double-edged sword’ (verses 3-4). ‘Her feet go down to death; her steps lead straight to Sheol’ (verse 5).

‘Keep your path far from her; do not go near the door of her house’ (verse 8). Otherwise the son will give away his strength and his years, and strangers will feast on his wealth (verses 9-10).

Then the father lets his son hear his own future voice, at the end of a wasted life: “How I hated discipline, and my heart despised reproof! I did not listen to the voice of my teachers or incline my ear to my mentors. I am on the brink of utter ruin in the midst of the whole assembly” (verses 12-14).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 2 introduced this woman briefly. Chapters 5 to 7 return to her at length, which makes faithfulness in marriage the most developed practical subject of the book's opening chapters. Behind it stands the seventh commandment.

Forbidden translates zarah, a stranger, someone outside the proper circle. Here she is outside the young man's own marriage, whatever her nation.

In the ancient world adultery threatened more than two people. It touched inheritance, property and whole families. Israel's law treated it as a crime deserving death (Leviticus 20:10; Deuteronomy 22:22), but Proverbs never mentions that. It speaks instead of what follows naturally: shame before the whole town, wealth and work lost to strangers, years wasted. The assembly of verse 14 was probably the community gathered at the city gate, where a man exposed in adultery lost his standing before everyone.

Wormwood is a bitter plant, a picture in the Bible of the bitterness of sin. The honey comes first and the wormwood after.

The man's speech at the end is a striking device. The son hears himself, years later, saying the very thing the father is trying to spare him: how he hated discipline.
passages.later: The command behind the whole chapter is short: ‘You shall not commit adultery’ (Exodus 20:14). And the New Testament repeats the warning: ‘Marriage should be honored by all and the marriage bed kept undefiled, for God will judge the sexually immoral and adulterers’ (Hebrews 13:4).
passages.hard:
Doesn't this chapter blame the woman and speak only to men?

The chapter is addressed to a son, because the book's opening chapters are written as a father's teaching to a young man, and they describe the temptation he will face. That is its frame. It is not a claim that men are innocent and women guilty.

In fact the chapter puts the weight of responsibility on the young man. He is the one who must keep his path far from her door, and verses 21 to 23 say that his own sins are what trap him. Elsewhere Proverbs speaks just as hard words about men who are violent or deceitful, and it praises wise women, above all in chapter 31.

Many readers apply the warning in both directions, since what it describes, sweet words, hidden costs, wasted years and public ruin, applies to anyone tempted to betray a marriage. The chapter's aim is not to make women into villains. It is to protect marriages and households.
passages.asks: The father lets his son hear his own future regret. Ask what you would want to be able to say at the end of your life about the choices in front of you now. And ask where you are being offered something sweet now that will be bitter later.

passages.happening:
Now the father turns from warning to invitation. ‘Drink water from your own cistern, and running water from your own well’ (verse 15). Why let your springs run out into the streets? ‘Let them be yours alone, never to be shared with strangers’ (verse 17).

“May your fountain be blessed, and may you rejoice in the wife of your youth” (verse 18). He speaks warmly of married love: may her love delight and captivate him always (verse 19). ‘Why be captivated, my son, by an adulteress, or embrace the bosom of a stranger?’ (verse 20).

The chapter ends with God. ‘For a man’s ways are before the eyes of the LORD, and the LORD examines all his paths’ (verse 21). ‘The iniquities of a wicked man entrap him; the cords of his sin entangle him’ (verse 22). ‘He dies for lack of discipline, led astray by his own great folly’ (verse 23).
passages.hearers:
Water was precious in a land that depended on seasonal rain. Families carved cisterns into the rock to catch rainwater, and a household's own well was valuable property. Letting your springs flow into the street would be pure waste. The father uses the picture to speak with restraint about sexual love: a husband is to find his delight in his own marriage, not scatter it.

This chapter is not only a warning. It celebrates married love as good and worth guarding. The phrase ‘the wife of your youth’ reflects a world of early marriage, where a man's first wife was the companion of his whole adult life. A doe and a fawn were admired in ancient love poetry for their grace.

One Hebrew verb ties the ending together. Shagah means to stray, reel or be intoxicated. In verse 19 it is good: be captivated by your wife's love. In verse 20 it is a question: why be captivated by another? In verse 23 it is the fool, led astray. A man will be carried away by something, his wife's love or his own folly.

And no one sins in secret. The LORD sees every path. Sin is pictured not only as a broken rule but as a cord that tightens around the one who ties it.
passages.later: The Song of Songs uses the same water pictures for a bride: ‘You are a garden spring, a well of fresh water flowing down from Lebanon’ (Song of Songs 4:15). Ecclesiastes says, ‘Enjoy life with your beloved wife all the days of the fleeting life that God has given you under the sun’ (Ecclesiastes 9:9). And Job asks of God, ‘Does He not see my ways and count my every step?’ (Job 31:4).
passages.asks: The chapter calls married love a gift to rejoice in, not only a rule to keep. If you are married, ask what it would look like to delight in your husband or wife this week. And whoever you are, ask what cords you may be tying around yourself in secret, since the LORD sees every path.
